title: Valu v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (No 2) — Federal Circuit and Family Court Refers Solicitor to the NSW Legal Services Commissioner over ChatGPT-Fabricated Citations and Quotes
pub: Valu v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs (No 2) [2025] FedCFamC2G 95
author: Judge Rania Skaros

dom.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts

kp.k: Unverified ChatGPT output introduced fabricated authorities and quotations
kp.d: The judgment records that the applicant's October 2024 application and submissions contained nonexistent cases and purported Tribunal quotations. The solicitor explained that time constraints and health issues prompted his use of ChatGPT, against a background of legal services promoting AI assistance. His account identifies reliance on fluent output without verification, rather than any measured assessment of AI accuracy.
qs: He accessed the site known as ChatGPT, inserted some words and the site prepared a summary of cases for him.
He said the summary read well, so he incorporated the authorities and references into his submissions without checking the details.

kp.k: Existing professional duties apply to AI-generated court submissions
kp.d: The Court found that filing fictional authorities and Tribunal quotations fell below the competence and diligence owed to the client and the practitioner's duty to the Court, referring to rule 19.1 of the NSW Solicitors' Conduct Rules. The solicitor's assertion that a subsequent AI practice note would have changed his approach did not prevent referral under the existing professional framework.
qs: The conduct also falls short of a legal practitioner's duty to the Court, including the duty to ensure that the Court is not deceived or mislead, even if unintentionally: r 19.1 of the Conduct Rules.
The ALR said if he had access to the Practice Note at the time he drafted the submissions, he would not have incorporated the material generated by AI.

kp.k: AI errors transferred verification burdens to courts and opponents
kp.d: The Court found concrete downstream costs: judges' staff spent considerable time seeking nonexistent authorities and checking the Tribunal decision, the Minister prepared reply submissions, and the scheduled 25 November 2024 final hearing was replaced by a directions hearing. Corrected documents did not undo this work; further timetabling was required before the substantive hearing on 10 December 2024.
qs: However, by the time this occurred, the Court and the Associates had already spent a considerable amount of time attempting to locate the cases and enquiring as to whether the correct Tribunal decision had been filed with the Court.
The ALR's conduct created unnecessary additional work for the Court and the Minister.

kp.k: Correcting AI errors also requires ordinary procedural compliance
kp.d: The solicitor emailed corrected submissions to chambers without his opponent's consent or copying the opponent. The Court treated this as a separate breach of rule 22.5, while accepting that exclusion was not deliberate and likely reflected unfamiliarity with litigation procedure and the Conduct Rules.
qs: The Court accepts that the ALR did not deliberately intend to exclude his opponent from communication with the Court and that the oversight likely arose from his lack of familiarity with litigation procedure and the Conduct Rules.

kp.k: Remorse and correction did not preclude regulatory referral
kp.d: The Court accepted genuine regret, prompt efforts to correct the documents once alerted, an undertaking to improve understanding of generative AI risks, and that the conduct would not recur. Nevertheless, on 31 January 2025 it directed referral to the NSW Legal Services Commissioner. This was a referral for preliminary assessment, not a final disciplinary determination; the regulator would consider experience, advancing age, significant health issues and remorse as possible mitigation. The Court anonymised the solicitor.
qs: The Court accepts that the conduct will not be repeated and that the ALR has undertaken to further his knowledge and understanding of the risks of using generative AI tools.
If the Court refers the conduct to the OLSC, a preliminary assessment will be undertaken to ascertain whether any further action or investigation is warranted.
Consideration of these factors and whether they mitigate the ALR's conduct will of course be a matter for the OLSC.

kp.k: Related cases informed the public-interest rationale for referral
kp.d: The judgment compares the matter with Dayal [2024] FedCFamC2F 1166, where fictional authorities and summaries came from an AI tool within LEAP Practice Management Software. It reports that Dayal drew on Mata v Avianca when discussing harms from false submissions and referred the solicitor despite a genuine apology and an expectation of no repetition. These are judicial incidents, not model error-rate evidence; the present solicitor used ChatGPT.
qs: The Court notes that in Dayal, the solicitor in that matter provided the Court with a list of fictional authorities and case summaries which had been generated using an AI tool within the LEAP Practice Management Software.
The circumstances of the present matter raise similar issues to those in Dayal.

kp.k: Evolving AI guidance strengthens regulatory monitoring concerns
kp.d: As of the judgment, the Court noted that the Supreme Court of NSW had issued generative AI guidelines, while its own court and others had yet to do so. It endorsed the Minister's prediction that misuse would become an increasing concern and concluded that notifying the regulator served a strong public interest. This is a prospective judicial concern, not quantified evidence of rising misconduct.
qs: There is a strong public interest in referring this conduct to the regulatory authority in NSW given the increased use of generative AI tools by legal practitioners.
While the Supreme Court of NSW has issued guidelines around the use of generative AI, other Courts, including this Court, are yet to develop their guidelines.

The Court agrees with the Minister that the misuse of generative AI is likely to be of increasing concern and that there is a public interest in the OLSC being made aware of such conduct as it arises.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Skaros finds that filing unverified AI-generated authorities and fabricated quotations undermined professional duties and created additional work and delay; she also predicts that misuse of generative AI will become an increasing concern.
pts.d: In this migration judicial-review proceeding, the solicitor incorporated ChatGPT-generated material without checking it. Judge Skaros finds that filing nonexistent authorities and purported Tribunal quotations fell short of duties to the client and Court, and caused unnecessary work and procedural disruption. The solicitor's account attributes his use of ChatGPT to time constraints and health issues, and his reliance to the output reading well; his counsel describes the output as seductive. These are explanations advanced for the conduct, not findings of AI productivity gains. Judge Skaros expressly adopts the Minister's prediction of increasing concern about misuse, and finds a public interest in regulatory notification as generative AI use grows. The resulting order is a referral for regulatory consideration, not a final disciplinary sanction. The judgment also addresses improper ex parte communication, a separate conduct issue rather than an inherent consequence of AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on the documented litigation incident, the solicitor's admissions, the Court's experience of corrective work, and an analogous judicial decision—not measured model error rates or market data.
pts.d: The judgment reproduces the Minister's identification of 17 nonexistent cited decisions and purported quotations in eight numbered submission paragraphs. It records the solicitor's admission that he used AI and did not verify the material, and the Court's and Associates' efforts to locate authorities and check the Tribunal decision. The original final hearing was vacated, replacement submissions were required, and further timetabling followed. Judge Skaros also relies on the analogy with Dayal, involving fictional authorities generated using an AI tool within LEAP Practice Management Software; the present solicitor used ChatGPT. Mata v Avianca appears through the judgment's account of Dayal's discussion of potential harms. Professional-duty findings reference the NSW Conduct Rules. The prediction of growing concern is a qualitative judicial assessment agreeing with the Minister, with no quantified adoption trend or forecast offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The observed consequences arose in late 2024; the January 2025 judgment makes an undated forward-looking prediction about increasing misuse concerns, qualified by the evolving guidance environment.
pts.d: The problematic documents were filed on 23 and 25 October 2024. The Minister identified errors in November, and the scheduled 25 November final hearing was replaced by a directions hearing; the substantive hearing occurred on 10 December 2024. Referral was ordered on 31 January 2025. The concrete harm concerns reliance on generated material without human verification, not a claim that all legal AI use produces harm. The solicitor argued that the NSW Supreme Court's 21 November 2024 Practice Note post-dated his filings and would have changed his conduct had it been available. Judge Skaros notes that her Court had yet to develop guidelines. She accepts that this solicitor's conduct will not recur, while nevertheless finding referral warranted and broader misuse likely to become an increasing concern. No specific forecast horizon is stated.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected parties are litigation clients, solicitors, courts and their staff, opposing parties, and professional regulators; the judgment frames oversight as a public-interest matter.
pts.d: The migration applicant received representation below the expected standard of competence and diligence and experienced disruption to the proceeding. The solicitor faced a referral to the NSW Legal Services Commissioner despite accepted remorse and corrective steps; his identity was anonymised, and any further investigation or action remained for the regulator. The Court and Associates spent time searching for fictitious authorities and checking the record; the Minister had already prepared reply submissions and incurred additional work. More broadly, the judgment identifies regulatory awareness of AI misuse by legal practitioners as serving the public interest. It makes no claims about legal employment, firm staffing, pricing, market shares, or improved access to justice.
